title: Values and Data Types in Bash knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Values and Data Types in Bash”?
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Scalar variables” under lesson 40, “Values and Data Types in Bash”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Values and Data Types in Bash”?
options: Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
Use array elements to preserve distinct values; check Bash version for newer array features.
questions.answer_key: Use array elements to preserve distinct values; check Bash version for newer array features.
questions.explanation: Use array elements to preserve distinct values; check Bash version for newer array features. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Values and Data Types in Bash”?
options: Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation.
Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
questions.answer_key: Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation.
questions.explanation: Use a small reproducible example, test an edge case, and record both the result and an important limitation. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
